title: Population Ethics and Effective Altruism
subtitle: How many people, how happy, and how much do we owe?
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain the non-identity problem and why it challenges person-affecting views of harm.
By the end you will be able to state the Repugnant Conclusion, show how the total view leads to it, and explain why the average view and other alternatives fail too.
By the end you will be able to describe effective altruism, its main ideas and its turn to longtermism.
By the end you will be able to evaluate the demandingness objection and other major criticisms of effective altruism.
hook:
Most moral questions take the cast of characters for granted. Should I keep my promise to *her*? Is this policy fair to *them*? But some of our most important choices decide who will exist at all. Whether to have a child, and when; how a society invests, builds and burns fuel; whether humanity survives the next few centuries: these choices shape not only how future people live, but which future people there will be, and how many.

The branch of ethics that deals with such choices is **population ethics**, and it was transformed by one book, Derek Parfit's *Reasons and Persons* (1984). Parfit showed that our most natural principles, applied to these questions, generate paradoxes as stubborn as those of the Logic track. In this final lesson of the Ethics track we work through those paradoxes, then turn to **effective altruism**, a movement Parfit's ideas helped inspire, which asks how to do the most good with the resources we have, and whose ambitions raise one of the oldest questions in ethics: how much can morality demand?

sections.heading: The Non-Identity Problem
sections.body:
Begin with Parfit's own example. A 14-year-old girl decides to have a child. Because she is so young, the child will have a hard start in life, though a life still worth living. If she waited ten years, she would have a different child, conceived from a different egg and sperm, who would have a much better start. Most of us think she should wait. But why? Her choice does not make her actual child worse off than he would otherwise have been, because if she had waited, *he* would never have existed. The later child would have been a different person.

The same structure appears at the scale of whole societies. Parfit's **Depletion** case: a society can either conserve its resources or deplete them for a higher standard of living now. Depletion will make life much worse in two centuries. But such a large policy changes who meets whom, when couples conceive, and therefore which people are born. After a few generations, everyone alive under Depletion would not have existed under Conservation. So Depletion makes no particular future person worse off than they would otherwise have been. Yet surely it is wrong.

This is the **non-identity problem**. It targets a natural principle, the **person-affecting view**, which says that an outcome can be worse only if it is worse *for* someone. In non-identity cases, no one is worse off, yet the outcome seems worse.

Responses vary. Some reject the person-affecting view and adopt an **impersonal** principle: it is worse if those who live are worse off than those who would have lived instead. Parfit called this the **Same Number Quality Claim**. Others try to rescue the person-affecting view with a richer notion of harm (perhaps one can wrong someone by bringing them into a bad condition, even if they are not made worse off), or appeal to rights. The problem matters practically. Climate change (Day 88) is the Depletion case writ large: the people who will suffer most from today's emissions are, in large part, people who would not otherwise have existed.

sections.heading: The Repugnant Conclusion
sections.body:
The Same Number Quality Claim handles cases where the number of people is fixed. But what about choices that change how many people exist? Which is better: a smaller population with very good lives, or a larger one with lives less good?

The simplest answer is the **total view**, the natural extension of classical utilitarianism (Day 61): the best outcome is the one with the greatest total well-being, summed across everyone who ever lives. But Parfit showed where it leads. In his words, the **Repugnant Conclusion** is this:

> For any possible population of at least ten billion people, all with a very high quality of life, there must be some much larger imaginable population whose existence, if other things are equal, would be better even though its members have lives that are barely worth living.

If you multiply a very small positive amount by a large enough number, you can exceed any finite total. So a vast population living lives that are just barely worth living (Parfit's image is a life of "muzak and potatoes") beats a flourishing world of ten billion. Most people find this deeply implausible.

The obvious alternative is the **average view**: the best outcome has the highest *average* well-being. This avoids the Repugnant Conclusion. But it has its own absurdities. It implies that adding a person with a wonderful life is bad if the average is even higher. And, worse, it implies that if everyone already exists in agony, adding more people in slightly *less* agony would be good, since it raises the average. That cannot be right.

Parfit then devised the **Mere Addition Paradox** to show how hard it is to escape. Start with population A: ten billion people with excellent lives. Now consider A+: the same people, plus a separate group living lives worth living but less good, who affect no one else. A+ does not seem worse than A; we have merely added happy people who harm no one. Next consider B: the two groups merged, with equal well-being, slightly higher on average and in total than A+. B seems better than A+, since it is both more equal and better overall. But if B is better than A+ and A+ is no worse than A, then B is at least no worse than A. Repeat the steps, adding and then equalizing again and again, and we arrive at Z, a vast population of lives barely worth living that is no worse than A: the Repugnant Conclusion.

Philosophers have proposed many alternatives: **critical-level** views, which count a life positively only above a threshold; **variable value** views; and appeals to **incommensurability**. In 2000, Gustaf Arrhenius proved a series of **impossibility theorems**: no theory of population ethics can satisfy a small set of conditions that each seem compelling, including avoiding the Repugnant Conclusion. So at least one deeply plausible principle must go. In 2021 a group of 29 philosophers published a joint statement arguing that avoiding the Repugnant Conclusion should not be treated as a requirement for an adequate theory, a sign of how seriously some now consider accepting it.

sections.heading: The Asymmetry and Person-Affecting Hopes
sections.body:
Many people hold an intuition that complicates matters further, which Jeff McMahan named **the Asymmetry**. On the one hand, if a child would have a life of unrelieved suffering, that is a strong reason not to create the child. On the other hand, the fact that a child would have a wonderful life does not seem to be a strong reason to create the child. We seem to have duties not to create miserable people, but no comparable duty to create happy ones.

Jan Narveson captured this in a famous slogan in 1973: we are in favor of making people happy, but neutral about making happy people.

The Asymmetry fits the person-affecting view: no one is harmed by not being born, since there is no one to be harmed. And if we accept it, the Repugnant Conclusion loses its force: there is no reason to bring vast numbers of barely-happy people into existence in the first place.

But the Asymmetry is hard to defend consistently. If the happiness of a possible person gives no reason to create them, why does the suffering of a possible person give a reason not to? And neutrality creates its own puzzles. If creating a happy person is neutral, and creating a happier person instead is also neutral, it seems there is no reason to prefer the happier one, yet surely there is: this is just the non-identity problem again.

The practical stakes became clear when philosophers turned to the long-run future. If there could be trillions of future people, and if their existence would be good, then preventing human extinction might matter more than almost anything else. If instead we are neutral about creating happy people, extinction may be bad mainly for those who die in the catastrophe, a far smaller loss. Your answer in population ethics shapes how much you should care about the far future.

sections.heading: Effective Altruism
sections.body:
On Day 83 you met Peter Singer's drowning child. In "Famine, Affluence, and Morality" (1972), Singer argued that if you can prevent something very bad from happening without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, you ought to do it. Walking past a child drowning in a shallow pond to save your clothes would be monstrous; Singer argued that failing to donate to save a distant child's life is, morally, not very different.

**Effective altruism** (EA) grew from this argument and from the careful habits of thought of Oxford philosophers, among them Toby Ord and William MacAskill, who founded Giving What We Can in 2009, with members pledging at least 10 percent of their income to effective charities. The charity evaluator GiveWell, founded in 2007, had begun publishing rigorous analyses of how much good different charities do per dollar. The name "effective altruism" was adopted around 2011.

EA's core idea is to use evidence and careful reasoning to find the ways of helping others that do the most good, and to act on them. Several distinctive principles follow:
- **Cost-effectiveness varies enormously.** Some interventions do hundreds of times more good per dollar than others. GiveWell's estimates for its top charities, such as those distributing malaria nets, have been in the range of several thousand dollars per life saved.
- **Impartiality.** A person's suffering matters equally whether they live next door or on another continent, and many effective altruists extend this concern to animals.
- **Cause prioritization.** Compare causes by their scale, neglectedness and tractability. This led the movement to three main areas: global health and poverty, animal welfare, and reducing catastrophic risks.
- **Counterfactual reasoning.** Ask what difference your action makes compared with what would have happened anyway, a direct application of the counterfactuals in the Logic track.

In the last decade, many in the movement embraced **longtermism**: the view that positively influencing the long-term future is a key moral priority of our time. Toby Ord's *The Precipice* (2020) and William MacAskill's *What We Owe the Future* (2022) argued that because so many people could live in the future, reducing the risk of existential catastrophe, such as engineered pandemics or misaligned artificial intelligence, has enormous expected value. This argument runs directly through the population ethics above: it relies on the claim that the existence of future happy people is a great good, which the Asymmetry and person-affecting views deny.

sections.heading: The Demandingness Objection and Other Critiques
sections.body:
Singer's argument, taken seriously, seems to require giving until we reach the point where further giving would sacrifice something of comparable importance, which for most people in wealthy countries would mean giving away most of their income. This is the **demandingness objection**: a moral theory that requires so much must be mistaken.

It takes several forms. Bernard Williams (in *Utilitarianism: For and Against*, 1973) argued that impartial maximizing theories attack a person's **integrity**: they treat your deepest commitments, to your family, your work, your projects, as just one input into a global calculation, alienating you from what makes your life your own. Susan Wolf's essay "Moral Saints" (1982) argued that a life wholly dominated by maximizing the good would be strangely unattractive, lacking room for the excellences of a person who plays the oboe or reads novels well. Liam Murphy proposed that each of us is obliged to do only our **fair share**: what would be required if everyone did their part, rather than making up for the failures of others.

Singer and effective altruists respond in several ways. Some bite the bullet: morality may indeed demand much, and our discomfort reflects our self-interest rather than a flaw in the argument. Others distinguish what is morally ideal from what we should blame people for failing to do. In practice, most EA organizations promote a sustainable commitment, like the 10 percent pledge, rather than maximal sacrifice.

Other criticisms target the movement itself:
- **Systemic change.** Critics such as Amia Srinivasan have argued that a focus on measurable interventions neglects political and institutional change, whose effects are harder to quantify but may be far greater.
- **Speculative expected values.** Longtermist calculations multiply tiny probabilities by vast numbers of future lives. Critics warn that this resembles **Pascal's mugging**, in which a stranger promises astronomical rewards in exchange for your wallet: any small chance of a huge payoff can seem to dominate. Many effective altruists share this worry.
- **Ends and means.** In November 2022, the cryptocurrency exchange FTX collapsed. Its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried, had been a prominent supporter of EA and an advocate of "earning to give." He was convicted of fraud in 2023. The scandal prompted soul-searching about whether reasoning in terms of expected impact can rationalize wrongdoing, though EA's leaders had always stated that rights violations are not justified by good ends.

The question underlying all of this is ancient. Aristotle (Day 20) thought virtue was compatible with a life of friendship, leisure and partiality; Singer's argument suggests that, in a world with so much preventable suffering, we cannot justify ourselves so easily. Where you land shapes not just your theory but your bank statement.

keyQuote.text: We are in favour of making people happy, but neutral about making happy people.

modernConnection.title: Climate Policy and the Price of the Future
modernConnection.body:
Every government decision about climate change contains a hidden answer to the questions of this lesson. Economists who calculate whether it is worth spending money now to reduce emissions must compare costs today with benefits decades or centuries away. They do this with a **discount rate**, which shrinks future values. Part of that rate reflects the expectation that future people will be richer. But part can be a **pure rate of time preference**: counting a future person's well-being for less simply because it lies in the future.

This choice is enormously consequential. The 2006 *Stern Review* for the UK government, led by economist Nicholas Stern, used a pure rate of time preference of just 0.1 percent a year, arguing that treating future generations as less important merely because they come later is ethically indefensible. The economist William Nordhaus, later a Nobel laureate, used higher rates derived from market interest rates. Partly as a result, Stern recommended much faster and deeper emission cuts than Nordhaus. Here a philosophical question, whether time itself reduces moral importance, shifts trillions of dollars of policy.

The non-identity problem lurks too. Large climate policies change who will be born. If future people are not made worse off by our high emissions, because different people would otherwise have existed, then person-affecting views struggle to explain what we owe them. Most climate ethicists therefore rely on impersonal principles or on accounts of harm that do not require making someone worse off than they would otherwise have been.

Population ethics also shapes debates about falling birth rates, now below replacement level in many countries. Is a smaller future population a loss, as total views suggest, or a matter of indifference, as Narveson's slogan implies? Governments offering incentives to have children are implicitly taking a stand. As in every lesson of this track, the philosophy is not decoration on top of policy; it is a load-bearing part of it.

vocabulary.definition: The branch of ethics that evaluates choices affecting who exists and how many people exist.
vocabulary.example: Deciding whether a larger but poorer future population is better is a question of population ethics.

vocabulary.definition: The puzzle that a choice can seem wrong because of its effects on future people, though those people would not have existed otherwise and so are not made worse off.
vocabulary.example: The non-identity problem asks how depleting resources wrongs people whose very existence depends on the depletion policy.

vocabulary.definition: The view that an outcome can be better or worse only if it is better or worse for someone.
vocabulary.example: On a person-affecting view, failing to create a happy person harms no one.

vocabulary.definition: Parfit's name for the implication of the total view that an enormous population with lives barely worth living would be better than a smaller, flourishing one.
vocabulary.example: Accepting the total view seems to commit you to the Repugnant Conclusion.

vocabulary.definition: The view that the best outcome is the one containing the greatest total sum of well-being.
vocabulary.example: On the total view, adding a happy person who harms no one always makes things better.

vocabulary.definition: A movement and philosophy that uses evidence and reason to find the most effective ways to benefit others, and acts on them.
vocabulary.example: An effective altruist compares charities by how much good each dollar does.

vocabulary.definition: The view that positively influencing the long-term future is a key moral priority, given the vast number of people who could live in it.
vocabulary.example: Longtermism suggests that reducing the risk of human extinction is enormously important.

vocabulary.definition: The objection that a moral theory is mistaken if it requires excessive sacrifice from ordinary people.
vocabulary.example: The demandingness objection says that requiring us to give away most of our income cannot be right.

thinkingExercise.title: Test Your Population Principles
thinkingExercise.prompt: Discover which population principle you hold, then test it against your own giving.
steps: Rank these three worlds from best to worst, with a short reason: A (1 billion people with excellent lives), B (10 billion with good lives), and Z (1 trillion with lives barely worth living).
Identify which view your ranking expresses (total, average, person-affecting, or something else), and check it against one of the problems from this lesson.
Decide whether you accept the Asymmetry: is there a reason to create happy people, as well as a reason not to create miserable ones?
Look at the past year of your spending. Estimate what you gave to others and what you could have given without sacrificing anything of comparable importance.
Write a paragraph responding to Singer as honestly as you can: which reply to the demandingness objection, if any, do you accept, and what follows for you?

summary: The non-identity problem shows that many choices, from teenage pregnancy to resource depletion, seem wrong though they make no particular future person worse off, which challenges person-affecting views.

The total view implies Parfit's Repugnant Conclusion; the average view avoids it but has absurd implications; the Mere Addition Paradox and Arrhenius's impossibility theorems show every theory must give up something plausible.

The Asymmetry (we should not create miserable people, but need not create happy ones) fits person-affecting views but is hard to defend consistently, and it shapes how much we should value the long-term future.
Effective altruism, building on Singer's drowning child argument, uses evidence to find the most cost-effective ways of helping and has increasingly turned to longtermism and existential risk.

Critics press the demandingness objection (Williams on integrity, Wolf on moral saints, Murphy on fair shares), as well as worries about systemic change, speculative expected values and ends justifying means.

quiz.question: Why does Parfit's 14-year-old girl case pose a problem for the person-affecting view?
options: Because her child would never have existed if she had waited, so he is not made worse off
Because she has no right to have a child
Because the later child would be worse off
quiz.explanation: If she had waited, a different child would have existed. Her actual child is not worse off than he would otherwise have been, yet her choice seems wrong.

quiz.question: Which view leads most directly to the Repugnant Conclusion?
quiz.explanation: A large enough population with lives barely worth living can have a greater total of well-being than a smaller flourishing one.

quiz.question: The average view implies that adding people in great agony could be good, if they suffer slightly less than everyone already alive.
quiz.explanation: Adding them raises the average well-being, so the average view counts it as an improvement, which is absurd.

quiz.question: What did Gustaf Arrhenius's impossibility theorems show?
options: No population theory can satisfy a small set of conditions that each seem compelling
The average view avoids every problem
quiz.explanation: Arrhenius proved that at least one plausible-seeming principle must be given up by any theory of population ethics.

quiz.question: Jan Narveson's slogan, 'We are in favour of making people happy, but neutral about making happy people', expresses which idea?
options: The Asymmetry and the person-affecting view
quiz.explanation: It says there is reason to benefit existing people but no reason to create new happy people.

quiz.question: Longtermism's case for prioritizing the prevention of human extinction is independent of any view in population ethics.
quiz.explanation: The case relies on valuing the existence of vast numbers of future people, which person-affecting views and the Asymmetry deny.

quiz.question: Which principle is central to effective altruism's method of choosing causes?
options: Following the most emotionally moving appeals
quiz.explanation: Effective altruists compare causes by how large the problem is, how neglected it is, and how solvable it is.

quiz.question: Susan Wolf's essay 'Moral Saints' argues that:
options: Everyone should give away most of their income
A life wholly devoted to maximizing the good would lack other valuable excellences
quiz.explanation: Wolf thought a moral saint would have no room for the personal excellences that make lives rich, which supports the demandingness objection.

quiz.question: The Stern Review used a very low pure rate of time preference partly on the ethical ground that future people's well-being should not count for less merely because it comes later.
quiz.explanation: Stern argued that pure time discounting is ethically indefensible, leading to stronger recommendations for immediate climate action.

goDeeper.body:
A newer response to population paradoxes is to treat moral uncertainty itself as something to reason about. Since no theory of population ethics is clearly correct, William MacAskill, Krister Bykvist and Toby Ord, in *Moral Uncertainty* (2020), argue that we should act as a careful scientist does under empirical uncertainty: assign credences to the competing theories and choose actions that do well across them. This raises tricky technical questions. How do you compare the value of an outcome on a total view with its value on a person-affecting view, when the theories measure value in different ways? This is the **problem of intertheoretic comparisons**.

Another response comes from those who accept the Repugnant Conclusion. Michael Huemer, in "In Defence of Repugnance" (2008), argued that our intuitions about very large numbers are unreliable, since we cannot imagine a trillion lives, and that a life barely worth living may be better than we picture: on reflection, many ordinary lives might be not far above that level. Torbjörn Tännsjö defended a similar position.

Meanwhile, critics of longtermism have drawn on population ethics to argue that its conclusions depend on contested premises. If you hold a person-affecting view, or discount the value of merely possible people, the case for prioritizing extinction risk weakens, though many still think catastrophes would be terrible for the billions who would suffer and die in them. Critics such as Émile P. Torres and defenders such as Hilary Greaves have debated whether longtermism's "expected value" reasoning can be trusted when the probabilities are so uncertain. Greaves and MacAskill's paper "The Case for Strong Longtermism" offers the most rigorous statement of the view, and is a good place to test your own judgment.

readings.author: Derek Parfit
readings.note: Part Four, 'Future Generations', introduces the non-identity problem and the Repugnant Conclusion.

readings.title: Famine, Affluence, and Morality
readings.author: Peter Singer
readings.note: The 1972 essay with the drowning child, short and still forceful.

readings.title: What We Owe the Future
readings.author: William MacAskill
readings.note: An accessible case for longtermism, including a chapter on population ethics.

readings.title: Moral Saints
readings.author: Susan Wolf
readings.note: The 1982 essay in the Journal of Philosophy, a classic statement of the worry about maximal morality.

questions: Is the Repugnant Conclusion truly repugnant, or does it only seem so because we cannot imagine large numbers?
Should you give more to a charity that saves lives today or one that reduces a small risk of human extinction?
How much does morality require you to give, and how would you justify your answer to someone you could have helped?
